lead: A prestressed beam can be analysed in three ways, and all three give the same stresses. The stress concept treats the concrete as an elastic material carrying two forces, prestress and load, and adds their stresses. The strength concept treats prestressed concrete like reinforced concrete: the tendon is the tension and the concrete the compression of an internal couple. The load-balancing concept turns the curved tendon into an upward load that cancels part of the real load. Each one is the quickest tool for a different question.
prereq: You need the fibre stress formula and simple beam moments (M = wL²/8 at midspan).

blocks.text: Treat the uncracked section as elastic. With compression positive, a tendon at eccentricity e below the centroid and a sagging moment M, the extreme fibre stresses are:

f<sub>top</sub> = P/A − P e/Z<sub>t</sub> + M/Z<sub>t</sub>
f<sub>bot</sub> = P/A + P e/Z<sub>b</sub> − M/Z<sub>b</sub>
blocks.where: P is the prestress in N; A the concrete area in mm²; e the eccentricity in mm; Z<sub>t</sub>, Z<sub>b</sub> the section moduli for the top and bottom fibres in mm³ (equal for a rectangle, bD²/6); M the moment in N·mm; f in N/mm².

blocks.text: Two stages are checked with this formula. At transfer the force is the initial prestress Pi and the only load is the self-weight, which acts as soon as the beam cambers off its soffit. At service the force is the effective prestress Pe after losses and the moment is from the full load. The moment that makes fbot = 0 is the decompression moment Mdec = Zb(P/A + P e/Zb); cracking needs a further fcr Zb, with fcr = 0.7√fck. Between Mdec and the cracking moment the bottom is in tension but uncracked, and the formula still holds.

Think of the tendon force P as the tension T and the resultant concrete compression C = P as the other half of a couple. With no load, C sits at the tendon. A load moment M must be resisted by the couple, so C moves up by a lever arm

blocks.where: a is the distance in mm from the tendon to the line of action of C; M is the load moment in N·mm; P the prestress in N.

blocks.text: The line traced by C along the span is the pressure line, or C-line. Once its eccentricity ep from the centroid is known, the stresses are simply P/A ± P ep/Z. In prestressed concrete the steel force hardly changes with load, while the lever arm does; in reinforced concrete the lever arm hardly changes, while the steel force does. If the C-line stays inside the middle third of the section (the kern), no tension appears.
A curved tendon presses up on the concrete along its whole length. For a parabolic tendon with sag e measured from the chord joining its two end points, over a span L, the upward load is uniform:

blocks.where: w<sub>p</sub> is the upward load in kN/m when P is in kN and e and L are in m. At the ends the tendon also pushes horizontally with P and vertically with its slope component, which goes straight into the supports.

blocks.text: If w<sub>p</sub> equals the downward load w, the beam carries only the axial P/A: no bending, no deflection. If w<sub>p</sub> is smaller, only the unbalanced load w − w<sub>p</sub> bends the beam, and its stresses and deflection are found as for an ordinary beam. Designers often balance the permanent load, so the beam stays level for most of its life. For a tendon whose ends sit at the centroid, the sag equals the midspan eccentricity.

examples.question: A simply supported beam of span 10 m has a section 250 mm × 600 mm of M40 concrete. A parabolic tendon with effective force 600 kN is at the centroid at both ends and 150 mm below it at midspan. The beam carries its self-weight (25 kN/m³) and a live load of 6 kN/m. Find the midspan top and bottom stresses by (a) the stress concept, (b) the strength concept and (c) load balancing. (d) Find the midspan deflection and the sag that would balance the whole load.
steps: (b) Lever arm a = M/P = 121.875 × 10⁶/600,000 = 203.1 mm above the tendon, so C is 203.1 − 150 = 53.1 mm above the centroid. P e<sub>p</sub>/Z = 600,000 × 53.125/(15 × 10⁶) = 2.125. Top = 4 + 2.125 = 6.125; bottom = 4 − 2.125 = 1.875 N/mm².
(d) E<sub>c</sub> = 5000√40 = 31,623 N/mm². Deflection from the unbalanced load = 5 w L⁴/(384 E<sub>c</sub> I) = 5 × 2.55 × 10,000⁴/(384 × 31,623 × 4.5 × 10⁹) = 2.33 mm downward (w in N/mm).
Full balance: e = wL²/(8P) = 9.75 × 10²/(8 × 600) = 0.2031 m = 203 mm, which still fits inside the 300 mm half-depth with cover.
examples.answer: All three concepts give 6.125 N/mm² at the top and 1.875 N/mm² at the bottom, both compression. The tendon balances 7.2 of the 9.75 kN/m; the remaining 2.55 kN/m deflects the beam only 2.3 mm, and a sag of 203 mm would balance the whole load.

traps: Mixing signs halfway through. Fix compression positive at the start and keep it for every term and both fibres.
Ignoring the self-weight at transfer. It acts as soon as the beam cambers up, and it reduces the top tension.
Using the eccentricity at midspan as the sag when the tendon ends are not at the centroid. The sag is measured from the chord joining the tendon ends.
Treating w<sub>p</sub> as a downward load. A sagging tendon pushes up on the concrete.
Using the gross-section formula after the section has cracked. It holds up to the cracking moment, not beyond.

quiz.q: Name the three concepts used to analyse prestressed concrete.
quiz.a: The stress concept (elastic superposition), the strength concept (internal couple, C-line) and the load-balancing concept (equivalent upward load).

quiz.q: In the strength concept, what changes as the load grows: the steel force or the lever arm? Compare with reinforced concrete.
quiz.a: In prestressed concrete the tendon force stays almost constant and the lever arm a = M/P grows. In reinforced concrete the lever arm stays almost constant and the steel force grows.

quiz.q: For the worked example beam, find the decompression moment and the cracking moment at midspan.
quiz.a: Bottom prestress = 4 + 6 = 10 N/mm². M<sub>dec</sub> = 10 × 15 × 10⁶ = 150 kN·m. f<sub>cr</sub> = 0.7√40 = 4.43 N/mm²; M<sub>cr</sub> = (10 + 4.43) × 15 × 10⁶ = 216.4 kN·m.

quiz.q: A parabolic tendon with P = 800 kN and a sag of 200 mm spans 12 m. Find w<sub>p</sub>.
Find the top and bottom stresses of the worked example beam at transfer, when P<sub>i</sub> = 750 kN and only the self-weight acts.
When is load balancing the quickest method, and when is the stress concept needed?
quiz.a: Load balancing is quickest for choosing a tendon profile and estimating deflection, since only the unbalanced load bends the beam. The stress concept is needed for the code stress checks at transfer and service, for point loads that a parabola cannot balance, and at sections where the C-line leaves the kern.

beyond: Not for the exam. Analysis programs model tendons as equivalent loads, exactly the load-balancing idea, including friction and anchorage set along the tendon. Post-tensioned flat slabs are usually designed to balance a large part of the dead load. Search for load balancing of flat slabs and equivalent tendon loads.

figure.caption: The parabolic tendon of the worked example pushes up on the 10 m beam with 7.2 kN/m, so only 2.55 kN/m of the 9.75 kN/m load bends it. Superposing that net load on the uniform 4 N/mm² gives the same stresses as the stress and strength concepts.
